regenerable_on: nothing, and that is the point of the provenance above. These payloads were WRITTEN, not captured, so they regenerate from the committed bytes and from no machine. The shapes are not invented: a real estate publishing these three documents was captured on 2026-08-19 — 35 payloads, schema 1 throughout — and every member, nesting and vocabulary here was read off that capture. Only the CONTENT is fiction. If the schema moves, this variant must be re-derived from a fresh reading of a real host rather than edited to taste, or it becomes a corpus of a document nothing produces.
anonymisation_note:
Nothing was substituted, because nothing here came from any machine: the estate described is invented — two hosts named vault and annex, seven targets, two destinations — and the security prose was written for this variant. The real capture succeeded cleanly, is not in this repository and will not be: its manifest is 191 leaves describing what a private estate protects, where copies land and who may delete, and scrubbing substitutes the names while leaving the shape, which is the disclosure. Every other variant in this corpus comes from a disposable lab guest, and no lab guest runs an estate's protection layer, so this collector is the one place the choice was between an authored variant and no variant at all.

harness/scrub/protection.json exists anyway, and was PROVEN rather than written and filed. Writing a manifest is not the same as it classifying anything — traefik's first one bound nothing, because its paths carried the payload stem as a segment, and only the detector half of the gate had ever been executed. So this one was run, against a scratch copy outside the repository so the committed payloads and their anchors stayed untouched: it binds all 44 leaf paths across the 16 documents, and it substitutes the two host names consistently, INCLUDING inside the `<host>:<job>` reference strings under implementedBy — which is the structural consistency a per-file pass could not achieve and the reason the manifest is worth having before there is anything to hide. Running it taught two things worth recording: `~key` is its own path segment rather than a suffix, and `format: name` substitutes only names handed to the run, so an operator-chosen word nobody listed is refused as an unengaged substitution and belongs in `prose` — which takes the same free-text pass, and so still rewrites a host name embedded in a job name — the estate really does name jobs `<host>-appdata`.
note:
The corpus's first AUTHORED variant, and the standard it sets is that the shapes come from a real reading and only the content is written. Every member below appears in the real capture this was derived from; nothing was invented structurally, and where the adapter's behaviour depends on a value's vocabulary — `state`, `basis`, `result`, `class` — the word used here is a word the real documents use.

Authoring bought something a capture could not. All sixteen jobs in the real reading were `state: ok` with `basis: last-success`, so a captured variant would have exercised exactly one of the five states this subsystem exists to distinguish. This one stages five deliberately: green, stale, ran-and-failed, never-succeeded, and a restore that was TRIED AND FAILED. The last of those is the state the module docstring calls the worst and the easiest to fold into 'never tried', and no real estate is likely to be carrying one at the moment somebody captures it.

Three distinctions are staged as pairs, because each is one this collector exists to keep and each renders identically if a port gets it wrong.

ONE ROW, ONE VINTAGE. `document-archive` is `state: ok` with `lastResult: success` in the checker's verdict, and its own `last` receipt says `exit-code` with exit status 1, finished 25 minutes after the check. That is not a contradiction in the data, it is the design: the verdict is recomputed hourly and the receipt is written by the run, so a run that failed since the last check must not read as success. The receipt is the authority. A port that preferred the status row publishes `LastResult: success` beside a failure's exit status.

ABSENT IS NOT UNREADABLE. `runtime-state` has never succeeded, so its last-success receipt does not exist — the payload is the pair `[null, null]`, no document and no reason. `config-sweep` HAS a last receipt and it will not parse — the pair is `[null, "JSONDecodeError…"]`, no document and a reason. The first is a job that never got there; the second is a run that happened and left a record this host cannot read, and publishing silence for it would be publishing the row of a job that never ran. That is why every payload here is a PAIR rather than a document: capturing the document alone erases the only member that separates them.

OWNED IS NOT JUDGED. `music-library` is owned by `annex` and every other target by `vault`, which is the host name the `hostname` payload pins. Its opinions are therefore not evaluated at all — `opinions=None`, which makes no severity claim — rather than evaluated and found clean. The declaration is estate-wide and identical on every host, so judging a target locally wherever it is read would mint one condition once per host.

Stated bounds.

No hop chain is judged here and none can be. A target's protection spans hosts by design — the source captures, another host pushes the off-site copy — and `photo-library`'s offsite hop is `annex:photo-library-offsite`, a job this host does not run and whose receipts it cannot read. The weakest link belongs to the hub, and no host adapter can state one it cannot see.

The repositories themselves are never reached, by construction rather than by omission: reading the off-site one needs the delete-capable credential, and an observer holding it would break the estate's own rule that a source cannot prune its own history. Every fact here comes from a declaration, a verdict and a receipt.

One host, one vintage. A second variant from a host that owns none of the targets — where every row is facts with no opinions — is the other half of the ownerHost scoping and does not exist.

anchors_note:
Derived from the authored payloads before any stream existed, which for an authored variant means something slightly different from a captured one and is worth being exact about: the inputs were written first, and each anchor below was worked out from those inputs plus the adapter's documented behaviour — not read back out of a generated stream and enshrined. An anchor that failed on first generation was investigated rather than corrected to match.

The five document-archive anchors are the one-row-one-vintage pair, and they are the most valuable anchors in this variant. `LastResult: exit-code` and `ExitStatus: 1` come from the RECEIPT; the status row for the same job says `lastResult: success`, and a port that read the verdict instead publishes `success` and fails both. `State: ok` is anchored beside them deliberately — the job is NOT stale, it ran inside its window, and it failed. Green and failed at once is a real row, and a port that inferred one from the other cannot produce it. `LastSuccessAt` a different timestamp from `LastFinishedAt` is what proves the two receipts are read as two files rather than one.

The runtime-state and config-sweep anchors are the absent-versus-unreadable pair, and each carries the OTHER'S absence to make the pair discriminating. runtime-state has no last-success receipt at all, so `LastSuccessAt` is absent and — critically — `ReceiptsUnobservable` is absent too: a missing file is not a fault, and a port that reported one would alarm on every job that has never succeeded. config-sweep is the mirror: `ReceiptsUnobservable` carries the reason verbatim, while `ExitStatus` and `LastFinishedAt` are absent because the receipt that would have held them is the unreadable one. A port that collapsed the two payload shapes — `[null, null]` and `[null, "reason"]` — into 'no document' satisfies neither side.

CheckedAt and CheckedAgeSeconds are anchored together because the second is CLOCK-DERIVED, and that is the one number here a port can get wrong without touching a payload. The verdict was computed at 13:30:00Z and the variant's stamp is 14:00:00Z, so the answer is exactly 1800. The replay shim pins time.time() from that stamp; a port that read the real clock produces a number that changes every run, and a port that dropped the fact publishes a verdict with no vintage — which is the specific failure the fact exists to prevent, since status.json keeps its last good verdict when the checker fails to write.

FailedProofRungs and LastFailedProofAt on document-archive are the fifth state, anchored beside `photo-library` NOT carrying FailedProofRungs. document-archive has one proof and it FAILED; photo-library has one and it passed. A port that published the rung list from the proofs array without reading `result` marks both as failed; one that ignored failures marks neither. The absence anchor is what makes the pair separate those two wrong ports from each other.

OwnerHost vault and annex are anchored as a pair for the same reason: the hostname payload pins `vault`, and music-library's `annex` is what makes the ownership scoping observable at all. With one owner in the capture, a port that ignored ownerHost entirely would agree with the reference everywhere.

Independent false and true are anchored as BOOLEANS on the two destinations. `nearline-zfs` being false is the one a falsy test drops — the same shape as plex's `Refreshing: false` — and a port that published the fact only when true satisfies the offsite anchor and fails the nearline one.

The three commit counts are anchored because absence is not the only way to lose a collection. Seven targets and seven jobs are deliberately the SAME number and describe different sets — two of the seven jobs (`config-sweep`, `snapshot-sweep`) name no target, and two targets (`definitions-repo`, `scratch-space`) register no job — so a port that derived one collection from the other gets seven and passes, until it is asked which seven.

Deliberately NOT anchored: `unimplemented` and `unimplementedHops`. Both are present in status.json, both were carried over from the real document's shape, and the adapter reads NEITHER — no fact anywhere derives from them. They are in the payload so the variant is a faithful copy of the document the estate publishes, and unanchored so that nobody reads their presence as a claim that the collector uses them.
